[F11 F9 F10 F8] [RD-4]

This is a RydeTAXI trip billed by the meter (total $47.97 with a distance component of $33.33 for 23.64 km at $1.4099/km), so the extra 1.96 km of the unexempted segment went straight into the fare, and RD-2's metered branch applies.

No chat or in-app agreement exists: the record contains no rider-driver messages at all, so the rider never consented to the route change before the segment started (18:46), and the driver's post-trip statement cannot supply that consent.

The driver's 'breakdown, whole road was slow' excuse is not corroborated for the optimal route segment that was replaced: the only incident (F11, vehicle breakdown 18:27 on East Coast Parkway) is contradicted by the speed records for that corridor and Airport Boulevard, which show band 5 (40–49 km/h, free-flowing), not the band 1–2 severe congestion RD-4 requires.
The refund is the unexempted segment's extra distance at this trip's per-km rate: 1.96 km × $1.4099/km = $2.76 (SGD), as computed under RD-2's metered formula.

The excess distance billed (2.17 km = $3.06) exceeds the segment refund, but the residual 0.21 km within the 200 m route corridor is matching/return-traffic noise that RD-2 expressly does not refund, so the rider claims only the $2.76 segment amount.

The rider's own profile is clean (0 disputes and 0 upheld in 90 days), and the driver has 2 disputes in 90 days with 0 upheld, though no flag_account action is requested here since no prior route deviation has been upheld.

weaknesses: The rider's complaint overstates the facts — he says the app estimated 21 km and the meter came to 24 km, while the GPS records 23.6 km vs an optimal 21.5 km (F1) and the fare records 23.64 km (F6); the judge will use the system records, narrowing the claim to ~1.96–2.1 km of excess.

The driver's story is not wholly invented: there is a real LTA vehicle-breakdown incident at 18:27 on East Coast Parkway, 0 m from the optimal route, i.e. inside the 300 m matching radius and reported before the segment started (F11) — the judge may read RD-4(a) as giving at least partial cover for avoiding that corridor, so the strongest counter is the band 5 (40–49 km/h) speed data (F9, F10) showing no severe congestion rather than the absence of any incident.

There is no road-name or location evidence tying the driven 18:46–18:52 detour to any rider-specified road, and no chat at all (F7); if the judge treats the reroute as within a general 'fastest route' discretion rather than a specific unasked direction, the segment could be found not to be a deviation at all.

The refund is small ($2.76) and the base/distance/time breakdown (F6) is a meter total, so if the judge declines to decompose the meter on the RD-2 formula the case may end in no_action even though a route violation is recorded.

claims.assertion: The single off-route segment ran 18:46–18:52, adding 1.96 km (F3); the driver's reason for it was a vehicle breakdown, and the LTA incident feed shows a vehicle breakdown reported at 18:27 on East Coast Parkway (towards Changi), 0 m from the optimal route — inside the 300 m matching radius and reported before the segment began (F11, F9, F10).

Because the breakdown report in F11 sits on the replaced section of the optimal route and predates the 18:46 segment start while the trip window ran 18:35–19:10, the segment qualifies for the RD-4(a) exemption and no refund attaches to it.

The RD-4(b) corroboration is also present — the optimal route's roads ECP and Airport Boulevard were recorded at speed band 5 (40–49 km/h) covering 18:19–19:15 (F9, F10), i.e. below free-flow but not the band 1–2 levels that would independently exempt; this record is offered only as corroboration of the congestion on the replaced route.

No chat messages exist between rider and driver (F7), so the rider never gave route consent and equally never refused the driver's reroute; the driver's written explanation (F8) is not relied on as consent — it is used only to identify which incident in the LTA feed he was responding to.

Even on the rider's best case, the billed excess is small: the fare fact puts the excess distance charge at $3.06 (2.17 km × $1.4099/km) (F4); the 2.1 km total GPS excess (F1) is mostly accounted for by the 1.96 km off-route segment (F3), and no ERP/toll or unpublished add-on appears in the breakdown — total $47.97 = base $3.90 + distance $33.33 + time $9.27 + waiting $0.00 + platform $1.47, no surge (F6, F5).

No account flag is warranted: the driver has 0 upheld route disputes in 90 days (F14), so the RD-6 predicate (`route_disputes_upheld_90d ≥ 1`) is not met, and his 4.7-year, 779-trip record is inconsistent with a finding of repeated deviation.

weaknesses: The only incident in the feed, F11, is a lane-1 breakdown notice on the ECP; the driver does not show that it forced him 752 m off the optimal route, and F3 records an off-route excursion of that size, so the rider will argue the exemption does not reach the whole segment.

F9 and F10 record speed band 5 (40–49 km/h) on the ECP and Airport Boulevard — moving traffic, not band 1–2 congestion — and under RD-4(b) bands are corroborative only and cannot exempt a segment on their own; the rider will use F9/F10 to say the road was not blocked and the detour was unnecessary.

F8 is the driver's own post-trip statement that he took another way without asking; F7 shows no chat at all, so under RD-5 there is no consent, and under RD-1 the duty is the shortest and most direct route absent reasonable cause — the burden of the RD-4 justification rests entirely on F11.

Duration was 35.7 min against 28.4 min estimated (F2), which the rider will cite as corroborating that the detour cost real time and distance, and the meter is distance-based under the RydeTAXI model in RD-2, so any unexempted km converts directly into a refundable amount (F4).

events.title: Rider Advocate rebuttal: 6 points
events.body:
→ D1: The breakdown notice F11 is a lane-1 advisory ('Avoid lane 1') on the ECP, but the segment F3 describes straying up to 752 m from the optimal route — a lane-1 avoidance manoeuvre does not explain a 752 m excursion, so the incident is not evidence that the driven path was the shortest way round the incident. [F11 F3] [RD-4 RD-1]
→ D2: RD-4(a) requires the incident to justify the replaced section, and here the route the driver replaced was running freely: F9 records ECP at speed band 5 (40–49 km/h) across 18:19–19:15, covering the whole segment, so there was no 'reasonable cause' to leave the optimal route and the exemption in RD-4(a) does not attach. [F9 F11 F3] [RD-4 RD-2]
→ D3: The driver concedes band 5 is not band 1–2, and RD-4(b) says band data alone cannot exempt a segment: band 5 (40–49 km/h) is moving traffic, so far from corroborating severe congestion it affirmatively shows the optimal route was available and the 1.96 km detour was avoidable. [F9 F10] [RD-4]
→ D4: The absence of chat (F7) means there is no consent at all, and RD-5 puts the route-change discussion on the driver before he leaves the optimal route; a post-trip statement (F8) explaining which incident he reacted to cannot cure the missing consent, and the only message on the record was written after the trip and after the deviation. [F7 F8 F3] [RD-5 RD-3]
→ D5: The rider does not claim $3.06 or the whole $2.1 km: applying RD-2's metered formula to the unexempted segment only, 1.96 km × $1.4099/km = $2.76, and the residual 0.21 km is corridor/matching noise RD-2 expressly excludes. [F3 F4 F6] [RD-2]
→ D6 (concedes): The rider does not seek a flag_account — C7 already declines it on F14 — so this point is not contested; RD-6 is irrelevant to the refund, which turns solely on whether F3's segment is exempted under RD-4. [F14 F3] [RD-6 RD-2]
Revised ask: refund_partial $2.76

points.response: The breakdown notice F11 is a lane-1 advisory ('Avoid lane 1') on the ECP, but the segment F3 describes straying up to 752 m from the optimal route — a lane-1 avoidance manoeuvre does not explain a 752 m excursion, so the incident is not evidence that the driven path was the shortest way round the incident.

RD-4(a) requires the incident to justify the replaced section, and here the route the driver replaced was running freely: F9 records ECP at speed band 5 (40–49 km/h) across 18:19–19:15, covering the whole segment, so there was no 'reasonable cause' to leave the optimal route and the exemption in RD-4(a) does not attach.

The driver concedes band 5 is not band 1–2, and RD-4(b) says band data alone cannot exempt a segment: band 5 (40–49 km/h) is moving traffic, so far from corroborating severe congestion it affirmatively shows the optimal route was available and the 1.96 km detour was avoidable.

The absence of chat (F7) means there is no consent at all, and RD-5 puts the route-change discussion on the driver before he leaves the optimal route; a post-trip statement (F8) explaining which incident he reacted to cannot cure the missing consent, and the only message on the record was written after the trip and after the deviation.

The rider does not claim $3.06 or the whole $2.1 km: applying RD-2's metered formula to the unexempted segment only, 1.96 km × $1.4099/km = $2.76, and the residual 0.21 km is corridor/matching noise RD-2 expressly excludes.

The rider does not seek a flag_account — C7 already declines it on F14 — so this point is not contested; RD-6 is irrelevant to the refund, which turns solely on whether F3's segment is exempted under RD-4.

claims.assertion: The GPS track shows one off-route segment on 18:46–18:52, in which the driver covered 3.50 km where the optimal route covers 1.54 km, adding 1.96 km and straying up to 752 m from the optimal route — an unexplained deviation from the shortest and most direct route.

This is a RydeTAXI trip billed by the meter (total $47.97 with a distance component of $33.33 for 23.64 km at $1.4099/km), so the extra 1.96 km of the unexempted segment went straight into the fare, and RD-2's metered branch applies.

No chat or in-app agreement exists: the record contains no rider-driver messages at all, so the rider never consented to the route change before the segment started (18:46), and the driver's post-trip statement cannot supply that consent.

The driver's 'breakdown, whole road was slow' excuse is not corroborated for the optimal route segment that was replaced: the only incident (F11, vehicle breakdown 18:27 on East Coast Parkway) is contradicted by the speed records for that corridor and Airport Boulevard, which show band 5 (40–49 km/h, free-flowing), not the band 1–2 severe congestion RD-4 requires.
The refund is the unexempted segment's extra distance at this trip's per-km rate: 1.96 km × $1.4099/km = $2.76 (SGD), as computed under RD-2's metered formula.

The excess distance billed (2.17 km = $3.06) exceeds the segment refund, but the residual 0.21 km within the 200 m route corridor is matching/return-traffic noise that RD-2 expressly does not refund, so the rider claims only the $2.76 segment amount.

The rider's own profile is clean (0 disputes and 0 upheld in 90 days), and the driver has 2 disputes in 90 days with 0 upheld, though no flag_account action is requested here since no prior route deviation has been upheld.

weaknesses: The rider's complaint overstates the facts — he says the app estimated 21 km and the meter came to 24 km, while the GPS records 23.6 km vs an optimal 21.5 km (F1) and the fare records 23.64 km (F6); the judge will use the system records, narrowing the claim to ~1.96–2.1 km of excess.

The driver's story is not wholly invented: there is a real LTA vehicle-breakdown incident at 18:27 on East Coast Parkway, 0 m from the optimal route, i.e. inside the 300 m matching radius and reported before the segment started (F11) — the judge may read RD-4(a) as giving at least partial cover for avoiding that corridor, so the strongest counter is the band 5 (40–49 km/h) speed data (F9, F10) showing no severe congestion rather than the absence of any incident.

There is no road-name or location evidence tying the driven 18:46–18:52 detour to any rider-specified road, and no chat at all (F7); if the judge treats the reroute as within a general 'fastest route' discretion rather than a specific unasked direction, the segment could be found not to be a deviation at all.

The refund is small ($2.76) and the base/distance/time breakdown (F6) is a meter total, so if the judge declines to decompose the meter on the RD-2 formula the case may end in no_action even though a route violation is recorded.

claims.assertion: The single off-route segment ran 18:46–18:52, adding 1.96 km (F3); the driver's reason for it was a vehicle breakdown, and the LTA incident feed shows a vehicle breakdown reported at 18:27 on East Coast Parkway (towards Changi), 0 m from the optimal route — inside the 300 m matching radius and reported before the segment began (F11, F9, F10).

Because the breakdown report in F11 sits on the replaced section of the optimal route and predates the 18:46 segment start while the trip window ran 18:35–19:10, the segment qualifies for the RD-4(a) exemption and no refund attaches to it.

The RD-4(b) corroboration is also present — the optimal route's roads ECP and Airport Boulevard were recorded at speed band 5 (40–49 km/h) covering 18:19–19:15 (F9, F10), i.e. below free-flow but not the band 1–2 levels that would independently exempt; this record is offered only as corroboration of the congestion on the replaced route.

No chat messages exist between rider and driver (F7), so the rider never gave route consent and equally never refused the driver's reroute; the driver's written explanation (F8) is not relied on as consent — it is used only to identify which incident in the LTA feed he was responding to.

Even on the rider's best case, the billed excess is small: the fare fact puts the excess distance charge at $3.06 (2.17 km × $1.4099/km) (F4); the 2.1 km total GPS excess (F1) is mostly accounted for by the 1.96 km off-route segment (F3), and no ERP/toll or unpublished add-on appears in the breakdown — total $47.97 = base $3.90 + distance $33.33 + time $9.27 + waiting $0.00 + platform $1.47, no surge (F6, F5).

No account flag is warranted: the driver has 0 upheld route disputes in 90 days (F14), so the RD-6 predicate (`route_disputes_upheld_90d ≥ 1`) is not met, and his 4.7-year, 779-trip record is inconsistent with a finding of repeated deviation.

weaknesses: The only incident in the feed, F11, is a lane-1 breakdown notice on the ECP; the driver does not show that it forced him 752 m off the optimal route, and F3 records an off-route excursion of that size, so the rider will argue the exemption does not reach the whole segment.

F9 and F10 record speed band 5 (40–49 km/h) on the ECP and Airport Boulevard — moving traffic, not band 1–2 congestion — and under RD-4(b) bands are corroborative only and cannot exempt a segment on their own; the rider will use F9/F10 to say the road was not blocked and the detour was unnecessary.

F8 is the driver's own post-trip statement that he took another way without asking; F7 shows no chat at all, so under RD-5 there is no consent, and under RD-1 the duty is the shortest and most direct route absent reasonable cause — the burden of the RD-4 justification rests entirely on F11.

Duration was 35.7 min against 28.4 min estimated (F2), which the rider will cite as corroborating that the detour cost real time and distance, and the meter is distance-based under the RydeTAXI model in RD-2, so any unexempted km converts directly into a refundable amount (F4).

points.response: The breakdown notice F11 is a lane-1 advisory ('Avoid lane 1') on the ECP, but the segment F3 describes straying up to 752 m from the optimal route — a lane-1 avoidance manoeuvre does not explain a 752 m excursion, so the incident is not evidence that the driven path was the shortest way round the incident.

RD-4(a) requires the incident to justify the replaced section, and here the route the driver replaced was running freely: F9 records ECP at speed band 5 (40–49 km/h) across 18:19–19:15, covering the whole segment, so there was no 'reasonable cause' to leave the optimal route and the exemption in RD-4(a) does not attach.

The driver concedes band 5 is not band 1–2, and RD-4(b) says band data alone cannot exempt a segment: band 5 (40–49 km/h) is moving traffic, so far from corroborating severe congestion it affirmatively shows the optimal route was available and the 1.96 km detour was avoidable.

The absence of chat (F7) means there is no consent at all, and RD-5 puts the route-change discussion on the driver before he leaves the optimal route; a post-trip statement (F8) explaining which incident he reacted to cannot cure the missing consent, and the only message on the record was written after the trip and after the deviation.

The rider does not claim $3.06 or the whole $2.1 km: applying RD-2's metered formula to the unexempted segment only, 1.96 km × $1.4099/km = $2.76, and the residual 0.21 km is corridor/matching noise RD-2 expressly excludes.

The rider does not seek a flag_account — C7 already declines it on F14 — so this point is not contested; RD-6 is irrelevant to the refund, which turns solely on whether F3's segment is exempted under RD-4.

The segment itself is not in dispute — F3 records it — but RD-1 asks whether any exemption covers it, and the driver's reason is corroborated on the replaced corridor: a vehicle breakdown was reported at 18:27 on East Coast Parkway (towards Changi) at 0 m from the optimal route, i.e. inside the 300 m matching radius and before the 18:46 segment start (F11, F3).

Conceded as to the metered branch — a 1.96 km segment would convert to fare at this trip's per-km rate (F6, F3, F4) — but that only matters if the segment fails RD-4, which the timely on-route breakdown report in F11 rebuts.

Agreed that there is no consent: F7 shows no messages, and F8 is the driver's post-trip statement, which under RD-5 and G11 is not consent; the driver does not claim consent, he claims RD-4 reasonable cause, which needs no rider agreement.

F9 and F10 read band 5 = 40–49 km/h, which is degraded traffic on the optimal corridor, not free-flow, and under RD-4(b) bands are corroborative only — they cannot cancel the RD-4(a) effect of the lane-1 breakdown report in F11, which is the operative exemption.
Arithmetic accepted as arithmetic, but the $2.76 presupposes the 1.96 km segment is unexempt; if RD-4(a) applies the refundable amount is $0 and the correct action is no_action (F3, F4, F11).

The rider's own framing concedes that the residual 0.21 km is non-refundable matching/corridor noise (F4, F3), which confirms the whole claimed refund rests on the single 1.96 km segment the RD-4(a) exemption in F11 covers.
Conceded, and the driver does not request flag_account: F14 shows 0 upheld route disputes in 90 days, so RD-6's repeated-violation predicate is unmet and no account action attaches either way.

notices.text:
We reviewed your Tanjong Pagar Centre to Changi Airport T3 trip and found one part of the route was longer than it needed to be.

The GPS record shows a stretch of about 3.5 km where the direct route would have been about 1.5 km, taking you roughly 750 m away from the best path. Traffic at the time was moving normally and the only road advisory was for a different lane, so nothing justified the detour.

We're refunding $2.76 as a Ryde voucher. Your account isn't affected, and nothing further is needed from you.

We reviewed the route on your Tanjong Pagar Centre to Changi Airport T3 trip. One section of about 3.5 km was recorded well away from the direct route, with no congestion or road condition on the record that would explain it, and no passenger agreement to the route beforehand.

We've refunded $2.76 from that portion of the fare to the rider as a Ryde voucher, and the route deviation is noted on your file. No account flag has been applied. Please follow the suggested route where traffic allows.
